The somatic part of the levator palpebrae muscle is supplied by the oculomotor nerve and this is the part that is responsible for opening the eyelid. The autonomic part of the levator palpebrae muscle is supplied by the sympathetic nervous system and this part is responsible for pulling the upper eyelid taut in times of stress or excitement. If the somatic part was damaged the patient would be unable to open the eyelid. If the autonomic part was damaged the patient would experience ptosis. Ptosis is the drooping of the upper eyelid. The levator palpebrae muscle is the main muscle responsible for opening the eye. The levator palpebrae muscle has striated muscle (from the somatic nervous system) and smooth muscle (from the autonomic nervous system). The striated muscle is innervated by the somatic nervous system and the smooth muscle is innervated by the autonomic nervous system (both sympathetic and parasympathetic). Damage to the striated muscle would prevent the eye from being opened. Damage to the smooth muscle will result in ptosis. The smooth muscle in the levator palpebrae is innervated by the sympathetic nervous system, which is why damage to the sympathetic fibres will cause ptosis.

This muscle is responsible for opening the eyelid. Autonomic innervation: via the sympathetic nerves, this muscle contracts and holds the upper eyelid open. If somatic innervation is damaged, you cannot open the eye. However, the sympathetic nerves have a role in holding the eye open when you are looking down or in low light. If sympathetic nerves are damaged, you experience ptosis (drooping eyelid).

cands.text: Apneustic breathing is due to a lesion in the Pons (Apneustic breathing is a pattern of breathing characterized by deep gasping inspiratory phases followed by short, insufficient expirations.)Occular bobbing is due to a lesion in the Medulla oblongata (Also known as vertical sacades)Cerebellar signs such as truncal oscillation are due to a lesion in the Cerebellum (Also known as intention tremor)Bilateral Horners Syndrome is due to a lesion in the  Pons (Also known as eye bobbing)The absence of the corneal reflex is due to a lesion in the Trigeminal nerve (CN V) (Also known as corneal reflex)

Gasping inspirations followed by short expirations = apneustic breathing pattern, which is caused by a pontine lesion. Normally the pons regulates the breathing pattern and rhythm. In a pontine lesion, the pattern generated by the medulla is unopposed and so you get a pattern of deep inspiratory gasps followed by short, insufficient expirations.When rolling the head from side to side and noting that the eyes roll towards the side of the turn, this is a test for the vestibular pathway. The abducens nerve (VI) which innervates the lateral rectus muscle is affected in a pontine lesion, so the vestibular pathway cannot signal this muscle to roll the eyes towards the side of the turn. When lying normally and noting "bobbing" of the eyes from top to bottom, this is a test for the vertical position of the brain. This is caused by a lesion of the vestibular pathway in the pons, so the eyes are not being held in place by the superior rectus muscle.  The corneal reflex tests the afferent CNV and efferent CNVII nerves. When absent, this indicates a lesion in the pons or medulla oblongata.  From all of this, it is clear that the lesion is located in the pons.

The greater the resistance to airflow the slower the rate of airflow and thus the less air that will move in and out of the lungs. Compliance refers to the ability of the lungs to stretch. The more compliant the lungs the more air that will be able to move in and out of the lungs. Tidal volume and respiratory rate are the two main determinants of alveolar ventilation.

Alveolar ventilation = what actually reaches the alveoli, i.e. gas exchange. It is different to minute ventilation which is the volume of air taken in and exhaled. Resistance to air flow = how much the airways resist air moving in and out of the lungs.  COPD is an obstructive disease. This means that the airways are obstructed and so resistance to airflow is increased. This impairs alveolar ventilation. As Denise is struggling to breathe, she may be taking a bigger tidal volume, but there is a limit to how big it can be. She is also taking in more oxygen than she is using up, and this is contributing to her weight gain. This is because she is hyperventilation, and this means her blood vessels are dilating. This leads to her swelling up.
